stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Many growers in dry regions avoid planting living ground cover between rows of maize, reasoning that the extra plants will draw down scarce soil moisture. A three-year trial led by agronomist Farida Osei suggests this concern may be misplaced. Plots interplanted with a low-growing cowpea variety did lose slightly more water during early growth. However, the cowpea's leaves shaded the soil and reduced evaporation later in the season. By harvest, those plots held more moisture than bare plots and produced comparable maize yields.
choices: Cowpea plants draw more water from the soil than maize plants do during the early weeks of growth.
A trial suggests that ground cover between maize rows may conserve soil moisture overall rather than deplete it.
The leaves of the cowpea plants shaded the soil late in the season, which reduced the evaporation of moisture.
Interplanting cowpeas with maize raises yields in dry regions, which makes ground cover essential for growers there.
explanation: The passage opens with a fear that growers hold, and then says Osei's trial suggests that fear 'may be misplaced'. Everything after that point supports the reversal: a small early water loss, a later saving from shade, and more moisture at harvest. Choice B covers that whole arc, and its 'may' matches how cautious the passage is.

A.why: The passage says the interplanted plots lost slightly more water early on. It never compares how much water cowpeas use with how much maize uses. You turned a fact about whole plots into a claim about the two crops that the text doesn't make.

C.why: This is true, but it's just one step in the explanation. The passage uses the shading to support a larger point, that ground cover may save water rather than cost it. You picked an accurate detail that is too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: The passage says maize yields were 'comparable', not higher, and it never calls ground cover essential. You took a finding about moisture and stretched it into a stronger claim about yields.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Engineers are increasingly building sensors into structures so that damage can be detected before it becomes visible. The Kessel Viaduct, completed in 2019, offers an example. Fiber-optic cables embedded in its concrete deck register tiny changes in strain. In 2022, the cables recorded an unusual pattern near one pier, prompting an inspection that found a hairline crack weeks before it would have been visible from the surface. Crews repaired the crack without closing the viaduct.
choices: In 2022, an inspection of the Kessel Viaduct found a hairline crack in the concrete near one of its piers.
Embedded sensors like those in the Kessel Viaduct have made visual inspections of bridges unnecessary.
Fiber-optic cables were installed in the Kessel Viaduct's deck after a crack was found near one of its piers.
Sensors built into structures such as the Kessel Viaduct can reveal damage before it can be seen.
explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim: sensors let engineers find damage before it is visible. The rest of the passage is one example, introduced by 'offers an example', that backs up that claim. Choice D states the general claim and ties it to the example, so it covers the whole passage.

A.why: This is accurate, but it's only one event in the example. The crack matters because the sensors caught it early, and this choice leaves out that point. You chose a vivid, true detail instead of the claim the detail supports.

B.why: The sensors actually prompted an inspection, so the passage shows sensors and inspections working together. It never says inspections are no longer needed. You pushed the passage's claim further than the text goes.

C.why: The cables are part of the deck of a viaduct completed in 2019, and they are what detected the crack. This choice reverses that order, so the cables come after the crack. Go back to the lines about the cables and the 2022 reading and check the sequence.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Some linguists have proposed that when a borrowed word spreads rapidly across a language's dialects, the word is filling a genuine gap in vocabulary. Researcher Tomas Aaltonen tested this idea using regional Finnish newspaper archives, tracking twelve borrowed words from 1900 to 1960. Words naming new technologies spread quickly, as the hypothesis predicts. However, several slang borrowings that duplicated existing Finnish words spread just as fast, suggesting that filling a gap may be only one of several forces behind a word's spread.
choices: A study suggests that filling a gap in vocabulary is not the only factor that can make a word spread rapidly.
Borrowed words that named new technologies spread quickly through Finnish regional newspapers after 1900.
A study shows that whether a word fills a gap in vocabulary has no effect on how quickly the word spreads.
Slang borrowings spread more slowly than technology words did because they duplicated existing terms.
explanation: The passage sets up a hypothesis, reports a result that fits it, and then turns with 'However' to a result that doesn't. The conclusion is hedged: gap-filling 'may be only one of several forces'. Choice A states that limited conclusion, and it accounts for both the confirming and the complicating evidence.

B.why: This is true, but it's only the part of the study that matched the hypothesis. The author's point comes after 'However'. You stopped at the first finding and missed the turn.

C.why: The technology words spread quickly 'as the hypothesis predicts', so the study doesn't show that gap-filling has no effect. It shows gap-filling isn't the whole story. You took the hedged conclusion and removed the hedge, which made it far too strong.

D.why: The passage says the slang borrowings spread 'just as fast' as the technology words. This choice says the opposite. It names the right topic and then gets the finding wrong, so read every choice all the way to the end.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Forecasters at the port of Varela face an unusual challenge each autumn, when dense fog can close the harbor with little warning. Weather satellites often cannot distinguish the fog from low clouds above it. Only three ground stations record conditions along the coast, leaving wide gaps between readings. And the fog forms only when air temperature falls within about half a degree of the dew point, a margin smaller than typical forecast error. Together, these limits mean that forecasters can offer only probabilities, not firm predictions, of when the harbor will close.
choices: Weather satellites often fail to distinguish Varela's autumn fog from the low clouds that lie above it.
Adding ground stations along Varela's coast would allow forecasters to predict the fog with precision.
Several separate limitations prevent forecasters from predicting Varela's autumn fog with certainty.
Varela's fog forms across a wide range of temperatures, which makes its timing difficult to predict.
explanation: The middle of the passage lists three separate obstacles: satellites, sparse stations, and a narrow temperature margin. The last sentence, beginning 'Together', adds them up into one verdict, which is that forecasters can offer only probabilities. Choice C states that verdict and covers all three obstacles.

A.why: This is accurate, but it's only the first of three limitations, and the passage's point is what they add up to. You picked one true supporting sentence instead of the sentence that combines them.

B.why: The passage never proposes a fix. Even with more stations, the satellite problem and the narrow temperature margin would still be there. You invented a solution the text doesn't support.

D.why: The passage says the fog forms only within about half a degree of the dew point. That's a narrow range, not a wide one. Go back to that line; it is the reverse of what this choice claims.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: For more than a century, the dance suite known as the Harbor Airs was attributed to the organist Johann Reisl, whose name appears on its earliest printed edition. However, musicologist Adaeze Nwankwo has located a manuscript of the suite dated two years before that edition. It is written in the hand of Reisl's student Marthe Kolb and bears corrections that appear to be a composer's revisions rather than a copyist's. Nwankwo argues that Kolb likely composed the suite and that Reisl published it under his own name.
choices: The earliest printed edition of the Harbor Airs names the organist Johann Reisl as the suite's composer.
Newly found manuscript evidence suggests that Reisl's student likely composed the Harbor Airs.
Nwankwo's discovery proves that Reisl regularly published his students' music under his own name.
A manuscript shows that Kolb copied the Harbor Airs from Reisl's printed edition two years later.
explanation: The passage starts with the official credit to Reisl and then uses 'However' to bring in evidence against it. The author's real point comes after that turn: the manuscript suggests Kolb 'likely' wrote the suite. Choice B states that point with the same level of certainty as the text.

A.why: This is true, but it's the old view the passage sets up only so it can challenge it. You chose the information that comes before 'However' instead of the finding that comes after it.

C.why: The passage is about one suite, and it uses hedge words like 'appear' and 'likely'. It never says Nwankwo proved anything, or that Reisl did this regularly. You turned a cautious claim about one work into a certain claim about a habit.

D.why: The manuscript is dated two years before the printed edition, so Kolb couldn't have copied from it. The corrections also look like a composer's, not a copyist's. This choice begins with the right evidence and then reverses what it shows.
